items.note: Bhoja as the one ruler with strong historical evidence: own works, temples/images/buildings, copper plates and inscriptions, honoured by Vedic and Jain alike.
items.gloss: But a ruler whose presence in history rests on strong evidence, who wrote his own works, about whom temple, image and building construction is attested, whose copper plates and inscriptions survive, and whom Vedic and Jain alike honoured - only Raja Bhoja appears as such.

items.note: Bhoja's popularity and fame beyond India (Mongolian text), and his equal regard for all sects.
items.gloss: Raja Bhoja was popular across the kingdom and all India through his works, personality, conduct and generosity; his fame spread abroad, as a Mongolian traditional text on Raja Bhoja shows; he was a knower of dharma who recognised the worth of all prevailing sects and held equal faith in all.

items.note: Bhoja fought the Turks yet some verses are joint compositions with a Turk poet.
items.gloss: Even in fighting the Turks he made no distinction in creative work; verses jointly composed by Bhoja and a Turk poet are found.

items.note: Bhoja's legendary persona in folk song: a Malwi devi-geet.
items.gloss: Owing to his many-sided personality it became a saying that there was and will be no such king; stories and folk songs kept it alive; one Malwi devi-song tells how Villu Bai gives a son to a barren woman and had set right Bhoja's birth, praying to be treated likewise.

items.note: Interpretation of the Malwi song: Bhoja as the son of Mother Earth, loved by all.
items.gloss: Villu is a corruption of Vipula; Vipula is the Earth; the prayer is made to Mother Earth; Bhoja is earth's son; the whole earth was Bhoja's mother; with equal faith in all he was everyone's own.

items.note: Paramāra lineage: Sīyaka II, Vākpati Muñja (974-997), his younger brother Sindhurāja (997-999).
items.gloss: Bhoja was born in the Paramara dynasty ruling Malwa; until Siyaka II they ruled as Rashtrakuta representatives; his son Vakpati Munja (974-997 CE) became independent ruler of Malwa and expanded his realm; Munja's younger brother was Sindhuraja (997-999 CE).

items.note: Sindhurāja's conquests and marriage to Śaśiprabhā.
items.gloss: He defeated Kuntala Tailapa II, conquered Vagad after defeating the Hunas, took Kosala, then Lata and Aparanta, and in the south Chola and Murala (Kerala); he married Shashiprabha, daughter of Nagaraja Shankhapala.

items.note: Bhoja (999-1055 CE), son of Sindhurāja; copper plates and inscriptions 1010-1055; a plate signed in his own hand.
items.gloss: Raja Bhoja (999-1055 CE) was this Sindhuraja's son; several copper plates, stone inscriptions and image inscriptions of 1010 to 1055 CE are found; one copper plate ends 'this is the own hand of Shri Bhojadeva', i.e. Bhojadeva wrote and gave it himself.

items.note: Tradition of a 55-year 7-month 3-day reign over Gauda and Dakshinapatha.
items.gloss: By tradition Bhoja ruled 55 years 7 months 3 days over a wide region including Gauda country and Dakshinapatha, which suggests a long rule.

items.note: Bhoja's victories over named kings are engraved in the Udaypur praśasti (as the author says).
items.gloss: Following this policy Bhoja defeated the kings of Chedi, Indraratha, Toggala, Bhima, and also Karnata, Lata, Gurjara and the Turushka king; this is inscribed in the Udayapura prashasti.

items.note: Copper-plate colophons style Bhoja 'Maharajadhiraja Parameshvara Shri Bhojadeva'.
items.gloss: In the colophons of the copper plates Bhoja is called 'Maharajadhiraja Parameshvara Shri Bhojadeva' - clearly a king of kings.

items.note: Mentions Vidisha-Bhopal region's twelfth-century 'Mahadvadashaka-mandala'.
items.gloss: Moreover, from Vidisha to the Bhopal region there was a 'Mahadvadashakamandala' in the twelfth century, but it was the name of a single mandala.

items.note: Twelve mandalas under Bhoja when the Samarāṅgaṇasūtradhāra was composed; named mandalas.
items.gloss: Lords of twelve such mandalas were subordinate to Bhoja when the Samarangana-sutradhara was composed; notable mandalas include Avanti, Purnapathaka, Mohadavasaka, Arthuna, Sthali, Sangamakheta and Huna.

items.note: Bhoja's generosity; the claim that copper-plate grants exhausted copper may be hyperbole but not baseless; copper plates issued, some recovered.
items.gloss: Bhoja was supremely generous; it was said that fettering enemies exhausted iron and writing grant-plates exhausted copper in his kingdom; this may be exaggeration but not baseless, since history shows he defeated many enemies and issued many copper plates, some of which have been found.

items.note: Bhoja moved his capital from Ujjain to Dhārā for security and rebuilt it.
items.gloss: Raja Bhoja was a great builder; for security he moved his capital from Ujjain to Dhara and settled it anew; the newly built city became attractive.

items.note: Town-planning method of the Samarāṅgaṇasūtradhāra reflected in the description of Dhārā: moat, rampart, gateways, gardens.
items.gloss: The town-planning method Bhoja presented in his Samarangana-sutradhara has its literary form in the description of Dhara; traces of the Dhara he imagined can still be found; its moat, rampart, arches, gate-towers and gardens were all delightful.

items.note: Bhoja's great dam on the Betwa near Bhojpur (said to cover 250 sq miles), broken by Hoshangshah.
items.gloss: Bhojapur near Bhopal was founded in Bhoja's name, where a huge Shiva temple still stands; there Bhoja built a unique dam on the Betwa whose held water area was said to be 250 square miles; Hoshangshah broke the dam and emptied the lake.

items.note: The dam-lake: said to be the largest man-made lake, used for irrigation, with an island still a settlement called Deep.
items.gloss: Hoshangshah broke this dam and emptied the lake; it is said to have been the largest man-made lake and served irrigation; the island in its middle is still a settlement called Deep.

items.note: Tradition of 84 crossroads each with a temple in Dhārā; Bhoja's temples at Chittor and Kashmir.
items.gloss: It is said Dhara had eighty-four crossroads each with a temple; Bhoja built a temple at Chittor and one with Krishna at Kapateshvara in Kashmir.

items.note: Building revolution in Malwa from Bhoja's time; most surviving ancient Malwa structures are Paramāra-period.
items.gloss: From Bhoja's time Malwa saw a revolution in construction: palaces, temples, tanks and images; Mandsaur district is rich, Hinglajgarh a treasury of images; most ancient structures seen in Malwa today are of the Paramara period.

items.note: Bhoja's temples in the four directions and Mahākāla in the centre; confirmed by the Udayapura inscription and a Dhār Prakrit inscription.
items.gloss: Among the many temples Bhoja built were Kedara, Rameshvara, Somanatha, Mundira in the four directions of India and Mahakala in the middle; this is confirmed by the Udayapura inscription and a Prakrit inscription from Dhar.

items.note: Bhoja built Sarasvatī-kaṇṭhābharaṇa halls at Dhār, Māṇḍu and Ujjain following Vātsyāyana's prescription.
items.gloss: Bhoja built Sharada-sadana / Sarasvati-kanthabharana; Vatsyayana had said each town should have a Sarasvati hall for gatherings and plays; Bhoja probably followed this and built such halls at Dhar, Mandu and Ujjain.

reject_reason: Sanskrit verse in praise of Sarasvati and a truncated stotra description; no bearing on any unit

items.note: Inscribed pedestal of the Dhār Vāgdevī image (British Museum) with an unclear verse, artist's name and date; text of the lines follows.
items.gloss: The inscription on the pedestal of the Vagdevi image from Dhar, displayed in the British Museum, has an unclear verse, the artist's name and a Samvat; the inscription would run approximately as follows.

items.note: Translation of the Vāgdevī pedestal inscription: made by Maṇathala son of the sūtradhāra Mihira, written by Śivadeva, Samvat 1091.
items.gloss: Having first made the image of mother Vagdevi, a pleasing and fruitful worship-worthy image was made; made by Manathala son of the sutradhara (Mihira); written by Vivelika Shivadeva; Samvat 1091.

items.note: Dhār Vāgdevī image combines northern and southern sculptural traits; ornaments recall Bengal and Orissa.
items.gloss: It combines distinctive features of northern and southern Indian sculpture; its thigh ornament and cornet are of Dvishada style; arm ornaments recall Bengal and Orissa images; thus the image represents all India in its synthesis of styles.

items.note: Bhoja-period images mostly Śaiva; Samarāṅgaṇasūtradhāra prescribes iconography, forms and placement of images.
items.gloss: Most Bhoja-era images are Shaiva though images of other deities are also plentiful; in his Samarangana-sutradhara Bhoja discusses iconography and painting at length, saying which form of image should be where and specifying size and place of various deities.

items.note: Bhoja's well-organised administration and unique patronage of poets, artists and scholars.
items.gloss: Though war-drums sounded through his long reign, he was skilled in administration; officials ran their departments competently, so he could pursue art and literature; he was an unequalled patron of poets, artists and scholars, himself accomplished and a connoisseur.

items.note: Bhoja's forty-day festival every six months, scholarly debates, śāstra- and kāvya-parīkṣā assemblies.
items.gloss: It is said Bhoja held a forty-day festival every six months attended by poets, artists and scholars, who were honoured and given gifts; those wishing to settle in Dhara were accommodated; there were debates, tests of sastra and poetry, story gatherings and samasya-purti.

items.note: Bhoja held such assemblies, authored and inspired works; Dhārā became a city of learning.
items.gloss: Raja Bhoja also held such assemblies and himself wrote works on various subjects and inspired others to write; thus his city became a city of learning and his realm a realm of learning.

items.note: Scholars of Bhoja's age (Dhanapāla, Amitagati, etc.); Uvaṭa and Purantaka at Ujjain; Jain scholars welcomed.
items.gloss: Scholars like Chitrapa, Halayudha, Bhatta Lakshmidhara, Dhanapala and Amitagati enriched the age; at Ujjain Uvvata commented on the Veda and Purantaka, priest of Mahakala, composed the Shyamaladandaka; many Jain scholars and saints appeared and Bhoja welcomed them.

items.note: Ballāla's Bhojaprabandha as the most popular of the many later works praising Bhoja - tradition rather than record.
items.gloss: Among these works the most popular is Ballala's Bhojaprabandha, with short anecdotes about Bhoja, Kalidasa and many other poets, which together create a poetic atmosphere.

items.note: Anecdote: the weaver compelled to compose a verse before Bhoja's court; illustrates the legend of Dhārā's poetic culture.
items.gloss: A poet needed lodging; the king ordered that the house of anyone in Dhara who did not compose poetry be given to this poet; officials brought a weaver, who composed a striking verse in the royal court.

items.note: According to Ballāla, 500 poets at Bhoja's court.
items.gloss: According to Ballala Raja Bhoja's court had five hundred poets; apart from Ballala various poets composed Bhojaprabandhas.

items.note: List of later Bhojaprabandha works with dates (1340, 1460 CE; 12th-century Vatsarāja).
items.gloss: Shubhashila's Bhojaprabandha shares stories with Ballala's; Ratnanandana Gani (1340 CE) and Ratnamandira Gani (1460 CE) wrote Bhojaprabandhas (the latter in seven sections); Padmagupta, Rajashekhara (Suri?) and Vatsaraja (twelfth century) are also mentioned.

items.note: Bhoja appears in Rajasthani, Avadhi etc. literature with both real and imagined stories - later tradition.
items.gloss: Bhoja is present in verse works in various languages including Rajasthani and Avadhi; Jayasi's Padmavat, Dayaldas's Panwar-vansh-darpan, Bankidas's khyat, Maldev's Bhojacharitra and others contain both real and imagined tales of Raja Bhoja.

items.note: Malwi traditional doha in which an old woman converses with Bhoja: 'Dhārā too will go, do not be proud, Bhoja'.
items.gloss: A conversation of an old woman with Raja Bhoja is found in traditional Malwi couplets; roughly: Raja Bhoja asks what the old woman has lost on Dhara's road; she answers she has gone from Dhara and none knows; Dhara too will go, do not be proud, Bhoja.
